question: Six worries about mixing medicines with food, drink or each other. Which are real risks, and which are overblown?
answer: The real dangers are the quiet ones. Grapefruit, milk and a second packet of paracetamol all look harmless, and each changes how much drug reaches the blood. The famous fears, the pint and the old pill bottle, matter far less. A pharmacist knows which is which, and asking costs nothing.
move: Worry about what changes the dose, not about what sounds dangerous.
ask: What do I take alongside my medicines that I have never mentioned to a pharmacist?

items.note: Juice with a statin such as simvastatin.
items.verdict: It blocks a gut enzyme, so several times more of the drug reaches the blood.

items.note: Painkiller tablets two years past the date.
items.verdict: US military tests found most kept working years on. Not insulin or liquids.

items.note: A cold-and-flu powder with paracetamol tablets.
items.verdict: Many cold remedies already contain paracetamol. Doubling up harms the liver.

items.note: Beer while on most common antibiotics.
items.verdict: Fine in moderation with most. The NHS warns off metronidazole and tinidazole.

items.note: Swallowing ciprofloxacin with a glass of milk.
items.verdict: Calcium binds the drug in the gut, so much less of it is absorbed.

items.note: Ibuprofen and paracetamol together, each at normal dose.
items.verdict: They work differently. Adults can safely take both at the same time.

source: NHS medicines guidance; Lyon et al., 2006
reference: NHS, Can I drink alcohol while taking antibiotics?; NHS, Ciprofloxacin: how and when to take it; NHS, Paracetamol for adults; Lyon et al., Stability profiles of drug products extended beyond labeled expiration dates, Journal of Pharmaceutical Sciences 95:1549, 2006; Lilja et al., Clin Pharmacol Ther 64:477, 1998
